title: How To Turn Your Classroom From Failure To Excellence
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that accepting less than what a teacher asks of students — talking over them, tolerating shoddy work, ignoring off-task behavior — is a quiet, cumulative form of failure that erodes standards and tells students they are a lost cause. He rejects the common objection that fixing every lapse costs too much time, arguing instead that well-executed routines and transitions save enormous time compared to repeatedly tolerating poor execution. His five-step method for setting students up to actually meet high standards is: be highly detailed in expectations, model precisely, remind before misbehavior can occur (never after), redo any poorly performed routine by returning to the prior transition, and double-check understanding before releasing students to work independently. He closes by describing the compounding effect of a 'never moving on' standard: it builds a felt sense of purpose and belonging in students that ultimately transitions from an early-year hassle into an internalized identity.
points: Accepting less than what is asked — talking over students, tolerating shoddy work — is a quiet, cumulative form of failure.
Fixing lapses immediately actually saves time overall because well-executed routines eliminate ongoing disruption.
The five-step method: be highly detailed, model precisely, remind before misbehavior (never after), redo poor performance, and double-check understanding.
Reminders after misbehavior are discouraged (a consequence should follow instead); reminders before misbehavior are encouraged.
A 'never moving on' standard builds a felt sense of purpose and belonging that becomes internalized as part of students' identity.
quotes: Although in the moment it doesn’t seem like a big deal, accepting less than what you ask of your students is a form of failure.
In fact, moving on in the face of any deviation from what you expect is inviting an accelerating decline of standards.
Nothing saves time more than well-done routines, transitions, activities, group and independent practices . . . you name it.
Reminders after misbehavior are always bad (enforce a consequence instead). Reminders before misbehavior can happen are good and most effective.
If in the rare case your students perform poorly after following the steps above, stop immediately, rewind back to the previous transition, and start again.
Once you develop the reputation for accepting only excellence, then that’s what you’ll get. Success begets success.
